item.title: Russian hacker group Laundry Bear exploits Zimbra zero-click flaw to target Western government, critical infrastructure
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 state-sponsored group Laundry Bear exploited Zimbra CVE-2025-66376 as a zero-day since July 2025, targeting Western government, defense, and critical infrastructure via zero-click email to steal credentials and 2FA tokens.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-66376 is a CSS @import sanitization flaw in ZCS. Laundry Bear weaponized it months before NVD publication on Jan. 5, 2026. Payload is Base64-encoded JavaScript hidden in an SVG onload attribute, XOR-obfuscated to rotate signatures easily. Victim only needs to view the email; no click required.
- The custom tool "Ulej" executes 12 async exfiltration stages: harvests email address via Zimbra SOAP, injects hidden login fields to trigger password manager autofill, steals 2FA scratch codes, and creates app-specific IMAP passwords to maintain persistent mailbox access that bypasses MFA entirely. All exfil over HTTPS, no DNS.
- Stolen data stages to actor-controlled VPS running "Flowerbed," Laundry Bear's collection framework, before onward exfiltration to internal infrastructure. Phishing emails originate from previously compromised accounts to evade anti-phishing controls.
- Patch immediately: CVE-2025-66376 is fixed in ZCS 10.1.13 and 10.0.18. If patching is blocked, abandon the Classic webmail client now. Monitor for newly created app-specific IMAP passwords and unexpected IMAP sessions as a key post-compromise indicator.
Full IOC list and mitigation guidance are in the joint CISA/NSA/FBI advisory.

item.title: Detections Digest #20260727
item.description:
Weekly detection engineering roundup covers new Sigma, Splunk, Sublime Security, and KQL rules spanning WordPress exploitation, Linux privilege escalation, and email-based social engineering.
- Sigma added 3 rules for wp2shell activity targeting WordPress CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137. Rules flag HTTP POST requests to the REST batch endpoint, the hardcoded "wp2shell" User-Agent string, and web server log access to the dropped webshell plugin. If you run WordPress infrastructure, these cover both the exploitation attempt and post-exploitation access in a single chain.
- Splunk added 3 Linux rules tied to CVE-2026-46331 and broader privesc techniques: syslog kernel warnings for act_pedit out-of-bounds buffer writes, auditd execve syscalls correlated with PAM events catching non-root to root UID transitions that bypass sudo/su, and aa-exec abusing AppArmor userns profiles to run binaries outside standard paths.
- Sublime Security added 5 rules and updated 2. New coverage hits Zohodesk job scams, FileMail callback scams, ScreenConnect installer delivery via URLs with e=Access and y=Guest parameters, and Anthropic/Claude brand impersonation from domains under 90 days old. Updates reduce false positives on HTML padding evasion and expand Dotloop impersonation coverage.

item.title: Azure VM Command Execution using Third-Party Extensions – Salt Minion
item.description:
Abusing the Salt Minion Azure VM extension lets an attacker with extensions/write push arbitrary commands as root via a rogue Salt Master, with no licensing or cookbook infra required.
Key findings:
- Any principal holding Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write (Owner, Contributor, Virtual Machine Contributor, Log Analytics Contributor, and several lesser-known roles like Defender Servers P1/P2 and VM Restore Operator) can deploy the Salt Minion extension (publisher: turtletraction.oss) pointing at an attacker-controlled master. The minion calls out over ZeroMQ on ports 4505/4506, accepts the master key, and executes pushed states as root/SYSTEM with no interactive session.
- The demo payload hits the IMDS endpoint at 169.254.169[.]254 to steal the VM Managed Identity OAuth token, then exfiltrates it outbound. Once the minion key is accepted, arbitrary cmd.run commands run without deploying a new state file at all.
- On Linux, forensic gold is in /var/log/salt/minion. Grep for cmd.run to see every executed command with timestamps and job IDs. Auditd confirms execution: uid=0, auid=4294967295 (no login session), tty=(none), with salt-minion python process as the ancestor via ppid tracing. On Windows, watch for the Salt Minion python process spawning cmd.exe.
- Azure Activity Log is your first pivot.

item.title: From Virtual Share to Physical Shell: Leveraging Windows’ Inconsistent Access Control for LPE
item.description:
Two chained flaws in Windows storvsp.sys (CVE-2025-59517 + CVE-2025-64673) let a low-privileged user write arbitrary files to C:\Windows\System32 and escalate to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Patched December 2025; requires Virtual Machine Platform feature enabled.
Key details:
- CVE-2025-59517 is in VspVsmbFileCreate() inside storvsp.sys. Opening a vSMB path via CreateFileW() with FILE_READ_DATA only causes IoCreateFileEx() to use OBJ_KERNEL_HANDLE without OBJ_FORCE_ACCESS_CHECK, so NTFS ACL checks are bypassed entirely and the impersonation token is ignored. Result: a privileged share handle to any directory, including C:\Windows\System32, with HasWriteAccess left unset.
- CVE-2025-64673 is in VspVsmbHandleSetInformationFileRequest(), triggered by IOCTL 0x240330. When HasWriteAccess is unset, impersonation is skipped and the InformationClass is silently swapped to FileRenameInformationBypassAccessCheck. A crafted VSTOR_VSMB_SET_INFORMATION_FILE_REQUEST buffer renames an attacker-controlled DLL into System32 as wuapi.dll, replacing the legitimate file.
- Stage 3 invokes the IWaaSRemediation COM interface (CLSID 72566E27-1ABB-4EB3-B4F0-EB431CB1CB32) via LaunchDetectionOnly(), which loads wuapi.dll under a SYSTEM process. The payload DLL enables SeTcbPrivilege, calls SetTokenInformation to move from session 0 to the active console session, and spawns cmd.exe on the user's desktop as SYSTEM.

item.title: 84 Streams Later, Part 2: Inside Apple Biome
item.description:
Apple Biome on iOS 17+ holds 84 forensically relevant streams across five categories: device state, connected devices, geolocation, app usage, and app data. iLEAPP now parses many of them, but the ecosystem is far from fully mapped.
Key findings:
- Streams live in two paths: /private/var/db/biome/streams/restricted/ and /private/var/mobile/Library/Biome/streams/restricted/. Most have a 28-day active retention, but Device.Metadata and Device.Timezone have retained data up to 10 months, and Siri.Remembers streams (CallHistory, MessageHistory, AudioHistory) show records spanning several months, making them high-value targets on aged acquisitions.
- SEGB write timestamps survive even after record content is zeroed out. A zeroed record still proves the device was active at that moment, useful for timeline reconstruction when substantive content is gone.
- High-value streams for responders include: Location.Visit (arrival/departure, lat/long, place name, up to 40+ days), Siri.Remembers.MessageHistory (direction, sender handle, recipient, chat ID), Siri.Remembers.CallHistory (direction, contact handles, call GUID), Notification.Usage (notification content by app), and Wallet.Transaction (card name, transaction UUID).
- Device.Wireless.Bluetooth warrants caution: records list Bluetooth MAC addresses and names, but multiple devices appear under a single SEGB timestamp, so presence alone does not confirm a connection event at that specific time.

item.title: Helpdesk Hijackers: Teams Vishing, Quick Assist, and GoGRPC Backdoor
item.description:
Ransomware-linked initial access broker active since Jan 2026 targets corporate environments via Teams vishing, Quick Assist, and a custom Go backdoor named GoGRPC with four evolving variants.
Key findings:
- Attack chain starts with inbox spam bombing, then a Microsoft Teams call impersonating IT helpdesk, convincing victims to open Quick Assist. Once inside, PowerShell downloads GoGRPC to %APPDATA%\sekv[random].exe and persists it via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run under the name "Realtek HD Audio". The history is then wiped via Remove-Item on the PSReadline save path.
- GoGRPC (variants Lep, Giver, Pet, Kind, Jan-June 2026) uses gRPC over HTTP/2 on port 443 to a /agent.AgentService/Connect endpoint, unusual for a C2 implant since gRPC is typically used internally in frameworks like Sliver. Pet and Kind added TLS and method-name obfuscation. Execution log lands at %PROGRAMDATA%\appscreen\appscreen.log.
- Post-access recon runs systeminfo, whoami /groups, nltest /domain_trusts, and an ADSI searcher to count AD computers, all classic IAB pre-ransomware triage. S3Siphon exfiltrates Desktop, Documents, Downloads, and OneDrive to an AWS S3 bucket using user-agent BackupAgent/1.0, filtering files over 100MB.

item.title: Detection primitives for eBPF rootkits
item.description:
eBPF rootkits VoidLink, LinkPro, and Atomic Arch abuse a small set of kernel helpers to defeat ss, bpftool, and ptrace. Load time is the one window where defenders hold the advantage.
Key findings:
- VoidLink hides TCP connections from ss by placing a kprobe/kretprobe pair around __sys_recvmsg and calling bpf_probe_write_user() to inflate a Netlink message length field. The hidden message is swallowed by its neighbor; NLMSG_OK never trips because the inflated length still fits within the buffer. The connection vanishes without breaking the parser.
- LinkPro's Hide module hooks sys_enter_bpf and __x64_sys_bpf to intercept BPF_PROG_GET_NEXT_ID, BPF_MAP_GET_NEXT_ID, and BPF_LINK_GET_NEXT_ID calls, then fires bpf_override_return(ctx, -ENOENT) to truncate enumeration walks. Every program with a higher ID than the allowlist entry disappears from bpftool. A discrepancy between BPF_PROG_GET_NEXT_ID output and direct BPF_PROG_GET_FD_BY_ID lookups exposes this. LinkPro also writes "HIDING NEXT_ID: %u" to /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe on every interception.
- Atomic Arch kills debuggers silently. Its tracepoint on tp/syscalls/sys_enter_ptrace checks for PTRACE_ATTACH or PTRACE_SEIZE, looks up the target PID in a hidden_pids map, and calls bpf_send_signal(SIGKILL) against the calling process. gdb or strace crashes with no explanation.
- Load time is ground truth.

item.title: GitLab Users Urged to Patch After Research Reveals Critical RCE Chain
item.description:
Authenticated RCE on GitLab via chained Oj parser bugs: any user who can push and view diffs can execute commands as git, no admin or victim interaction required. Patch was silently shipped June 10.
Key findings:
- Attack chain: Jupyter notebook diff rendering passes raw repo bytes to Oj::Parser in a Puma worker. Two bugs, an out-of-bounds nesting stack write and a heap-pointer disclosure via truncated key length, are chained in a single diffs_stream request. Execution lands in system() with attacker-controlled arguments, running as the git account (T1190).
- Scope: GitLab CE and EE 15.2.0 through 18.10.7, 18.11.0 through 18.11.4, and 19.0.0 through 19.0.1. Versions before 15.2 used a different parser and are not affected. Versions 15.2 through 18.9 are out of GitLab's patch trains and will not receive backports.
- Impact: code execution as git exposes repository data, Rails secrets, service credentials, and internal services reachable by the application. Source-code disclosure, credential theft, repo modification, persistence, and lateral movement are all in scope.
- The patch shipped June 10, 2026, buried in bug fixes, not the security table. Operators had no signal to treat it as urgent. A working public exploit dropped July 24. Treat this as actively exploitable.
Upgrade to 18.10.8, 18.11.5, or 19.0.2 immediately. No configuration-only workaround is validated.

item.title: SIEM Bypasses: Diffracting the “CreepyDrive URLs” Sentinel Rule
item.description:
The community Sentinel rule catching POLONIUM's CreepyDrive OneDrive C2 has six exploitable logic bugs, any one of which lets an operator walk past the detection without changing their technique.
- CreepyDrive reads and writes C2 tasking through the Microsoft Graph API against a real user's OneDrive, making it look like normal Office 365 traffic. The widely-used Sentinel analytic (CreepyDriveURLs.yaml) fires on two exact URL strings plus two regexes matching /Uploaded/ and /Downloaded/ paths, all hardcoded from a single threat intel sample.
- The critical bugs: KQL's matches regex is case-sensitive by default, so lowercasing the folder name to /uploaded/ bypasses the regex branch entirely. Folder names (Documents, Uploaded), filenames (data.txt, response.json), and extensions are all operator-configurable and changing any one evades the literals. Item-ID addressing (me/drive/items/{id}/content) is a fully valid Graph API call the rule never sees. The beta endpoint and sovereign clouds (graph.microsoft[.]us) are uncovered.
- The structural problem beneath all of this: without TLS inspection on Graph traffic, RequestURL never contains the path, only the SNI hostname. Microsoft recommends bypassing inspection for Optimize-category O365 endpoints, so in many environments the rule is inert regardless of regex quality.

item.title: 84 Streams Later: Exploring the Evolution of Apple Biome in iOS
item.description:
Apple's Biome framework now spans 300+ stream folders on modern iOS, but most tools parse fewer than 20. A new deep-dive maps the full evolution from iOS 14 through iOS 26 and adds 84 streams to iLEAPP.
Key findings:
- SEGB first appeared in iOS 14 at /private/var/mobile/Library/Biome/streams/ and /private/var/mobile/Library/DuetExpertCenter/streams/. iOS 16 added a system-level repository at /private/var/db/biome/streams/. iOS 17 introduced SEGBv2 and dropped the public Biome area. For iOS 17 through iOS 26, all three restricted paths are priority targets in any full filesystem exam.
- KnowledgeC.db held 50+ streams in iOS 13 and 65+ in iOS 14-15, then dropped sharply to roughly 20 active streams in iOS 16 as Biome absorbed the rest. The migration was never publicly documented by Apple, but the artifact record is clear.
- Across four devices running iOS 18 and iOS 26, the author identified 84 streams with consistent forensic value covering app usage, Safari activity, location visits, Wallet transactions, Siri interactions, CarPlay, Screen Time, and message-related activity. Two streams flagged for future research: Siri.Remembers.MessageHistory and Location.Visit.
- Retention is not uniformly 28 days. Several streams preserve data for months, raising the evidentiary ceiling significantly.
Update iLEAPP to the latest release before your next iOS exam. The new Biome parsers are live.

item.title: Hackers Hijack Hotel Wi-Fi to Steal Microsoft 365 Credentials
item.description:
APT28-linked actors hijack hotel and conference Wi-Fi gateways to steal Microsoft 365 credentials via DNS poisoning, active since at least June 2026 across the US 🇺🇸, India 🇮🇳, and Saudi Arabia 🇸🇦.
- Attackers compromised Wi-Fi gateway management interfaces (exposed SSH, SNMP, web consoles) using weak or reused admin credentials, then poisoned DNS responses to redirect guests to credential-harvesting pages mimicking Microsoft 365 login. Fake domains include m365-owa[.]com and ms365-live[.]com. Targets span finance, law, healthcare, energy, and retail, anyone who travels for work.
- Hardcoded DNS resolvers like 8.8.8.8 do not protect you here. The gateway rewrites DNS answers before they leave the network. Encrypted DNS in opportunistic mode (the default) also fails because it silently falls back to plaintext, and that fallback is exactly what gets hijacked. Only strict-mode DoH/DoT or a full-tunnel VPN closes the gap.
- In roughly one-third of cases attackers also abused WPAD, tricking Windows into loading a malicious proxy config that routes all application traffic, not just auth, through attacker infrastructure. In a subset of cases they targeted the Microsoft device-code sign-in flow, walking away with MFA-cleared session tokens without ever needing a password.
- ReliaQuest links tradecraft, not shared infrastructure, to APT28 (Fancy Bear / STRONTIUM) via overlap with the FrostArmada hotel-router campaign.

item.title: Iran-Linked Actors Breach Are Targeting US Water and Energy Control Systems
item.description:
Iranian 🇮🇷 APT actors are actively rewriting PLC logic in US 🇺🇸 water, energy, and government facilities, disabling alarms and shutdown functions to create dangerous conditions operators cannot see.
Key findings:
- Attackers reach internet-exposed PLCs via OT ports 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, plus SSH over port 22 through modems. They use legitimate vendor tools (Studio 5000, EcoStruxure Control Expert, TIA Portal) to pull and modify project files, making malicious changes difficult to distinguish from normal engineering activity.
- The confirmed technique (T1565) involves downloading modified project files that preserve normal ladder logic but add overriding instructions that disable shutdown sequences and alarm logic. Operators see a clean HMI while the physical process drifts into unsafe states.
- Affected hardware now spans Rockwell Automation, Schneider Electric, and Siemens controllers deployed across Water/Wastewater, Energy, and Government sectors. Activity confirmed since at least March 2026.
- The Iranian 🇮🇷 group Handala has run parallel destructive operations, including remote wiping tens of thousands of devices at Stryker, demonstrating willingness to cause real-world damage alongside the OT intrusions.
Takeaway: Pull PLC project files now and diff them against known-good backups. Audit Add-On Instructions for unexpected logic. Block inbound connections on ports 44818, 2222, 102, 502, and 22 from any non-engineering source.

item.title: SharedRoot: Sandbox Escape in Claude Cowork
item.description:
CVE-2026-46331 in Linux's act_pedit module anchors SharedRoot, a sandbox-escape chain letting code inside a Claude Cowork local VM reach host macOS files. No confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, but a public PoC exists on GitHub as of July 23, 2026.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-46331 is a Linux kernel copy-on-write flaw in the traffic-control act_pedit component. CVSS scores differ by vendor: Linux kernel CNA rates it 7.8 High, Ubuntu and Red Hat assign 6.7 Medium. An unprivileged Cowork session user can create a user namespace, gain CAP_NET_ADMIN within it, and reach the vulnerable netlink path, no root required to start.
- The full chain: unprivileged code in the VM exploits the CVE to corrupt shared page-cache data, a privileged coworkd helper re-executes altered data producing guest-root, then guest root accesses /mnt/.virtiofs-root, a writable mount reportedly representing the entire host filesystem beyond just the connected Cowork folder.
- Affected scope is architectural, not a specific app version. The demonstration targeted macOS using Apple's Virtualization framework. Windows local deployments were not confirmed vulnerable. Validate the guest kernel version directly.
- Anthropic classified the researcher submission as "Informative" and host EDR cannot inspect inside the isolated VM by design, creating a detection gap.

item.title: 僵尸网络新秀：Dysphoria 演进与深度技术分析
item.description:
Emerging IoT botnet Dysphoria surpasses 200,000 bots in under four months, adding blockchain-based C2 concealment and a dedicated relay layer that makes infrastructure takedown significantly harder.
Key findings:
- Dysphoria evolved rapidly from jackskid and fbot variants (first caught March 25, 2026) into a hybrid architecture combining DDoS bots with a separate pure-relay sample (b0782a9...). The relay variant strips all attack modules and converts infected hosts into transparent epoll-based proxies, using UPnP to punch 155 ports through NAT and reporting status every 4 seconds to login.trees4sale[.]net:9000.
- C2 resolution abuses ENS and Solana SNS blockchain domains: burrberry[.]eth resolves relay node IPs via a "node" key, ukranianhorseriding[.]eth resolves infrastructure via a "network" key, and 24carnforth2merseyside[.]sol uses a "deserialized" key. IPs are encoded inside fake IPv6 addresses and decoded with a custom substitution function keyed to 0x80408454, returning real C2s like 144.31.38[.]215.
- The DDoS sample uses a heavily modified RC4: standard KSA followed by 5 rounds of LCG (seed 0xE0A4CBD6) shuffling, then a PRGA stage that mixes LFSR (poly 0xD800A4, seed 0xF31C8B2E) with triple-swap indexing and a rotate-XOR keystream step. Decryption key: 08 45 3C D1 F9 5D 5C 27 61 21 1C BD E3 0F 3B 9C.

item.title: CVE-2025-66376: Russian APT Exploits Zimbra Zero-Day
item.description:
CVE-2025-66376 (CVSS 6.1): Russian 🇷🇺 APT LAUNDRY BEAR exploited a Zimbra stored-XSS zero-day for mailbox theft across Western government and commercial targets, active since at least July 2025 and listed in CISA KEV.
- CVE-2025-66376 is a stored XSS (CWE-79) in Zimbra Classic UI's HTML email renderer. No link click required: viewing the message executes attacker-controlled JavaScript in the authenticated session. Root cause is incomplete sanitization of CSS @import directives combined with SVG-based event handlers and fragmented tag-split markup. Affects Zimbra 10.0 before 10.0.18 and 10.1 before 10.1.13. Patch shipped November 2025; CISA KEV-listed March 18, 2026.
- The script ran inside the victim's session and exfiltrated recent email (90 days), Global Address List, 2FA scratch codes, browser-saved credentials, and newly created application passcodes. Data left via DNS exfiltration to d-{ID}.{type}.{base32data}.i.{domain}/pixel.gif and HTTPS to js-{ID}.i.{domain}/v/p. Flowerbed framework infrastructure includes zmailanalytics[.]com (216.252.238[.]104), zimbrastat[.]com (64.226.124[.]190), and synacorzimbra[.]nl (216.252.238[.]64).
- Key post-compromise artifacts: CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest events in /opt/zimbra/log/mailbox.log with passcode named ZimbraWeb are near-certain indicators of compromise. Also hunt GetScratchCodesRequest bursts and SearchGalRequest spikes.

item.title: WP Botnet Master: How a Security Researcher’s Paid Course Built a 2.1-Million-Credential WordPress Botnet
item.description:

TAG-195 ("Golden Chickens") expands its MaaS toolkit with four new malware families, including a modular implant architecture that loads capabilities on demand to shrink its detection footprint.
Key findings:
- TinyEgg is a lightweight initial-access backdoor handling host profiling, interactive shell, and persistence. ChonkyChicken builds on it with browser credential theft, session automation, credential-backed remote execution, and network recon. All four families share Run key persistence under a consistent value name, filename execution gating, string obfuscation, and payload delivery via a legitimate Windows binary.
- The modularized ChonkyChicken variant uses a controller-and-plugin design: a base implant requests and loads at least 14 capability modules on demand from attacker infrastructure. This deliberately reduces the static detection surface of the base implant while letting operators provision only the capabilities each intrusion needs.
- ChromEggscalator is a modified version of a publicly available Chrome encryption-bypass tool, repurposed as a browser credential theft helper inside the TAG-195 ecosystem.
- TAG-127 is an observed operator and customer, deploying TinyEgg via ClickFix-style campaigns: fake security verification pages trick victims into manually running malicious commands that pull and install payloads through a legitimate Windows system utility.

item.title: CVE-2026-16232: Critical Check Point SmartConsole Authentication Bypass Exploited in the Wild
item.description:
CVE-2026-16232, a critical CVSS 9.1 authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole, is actively exploited in the wild and added to CISA KEV with a July 25 remediation deadline. Three days to act.
- CVE-2026-16232 (CWE-287) lets an unauthenticated remote attacker steal an application login token and authenticate to the Management Server with full admin rights. From there, an attacker can rewrite security policies across all managed gateways, alter admin accounts, manipulate VPN configs, and suppress logging. Compromise of the management plane is a force-multiplier: every firewall it controls is now suspect.
- Two companion CVEs ship in the same advisory: CVE-2026-62144 (CVSS 9.1), a management authentication bypass with privilege escalation, and CVE-2026-62145 (CVSS 7.5), a local privilege escalation in GaiaOS WebUI. Neither has known exploitation yet, but patch all three.
- Exploitation is confirmed pre-patch. Check Point published Jumbo Hotfixes on July 22. Fix versions: R82.10 Take 36+, R82 Take 118+, R81.20 Take 158+. Older branches (R81.10 and below) have no fix specified. Smart-1 Cloud is already protected.

item.title: Microsoft DART Investigates a SharePoint Breach Involving Two Separate Threat Actors
item.description:
Microsoft DART investigated a ransomware breach of on-premises SharePoint servers where two separate threat actors were found operating simultaneously, exploiting CVE-2025-49706 and CVE-2025-49704.
Key findings:
- Storm-2603, assessed as China-based, exploited CVE-2025-49706 (SharePoint auth spoofing) and CVE-2025-49704 (SharePoint code injection) to gain initial access, then used Velociraptor at SYSTEM-level for recon, blending into trusted admin behavior. Remote access was maintained via Cloudflare tunneling, Zoho Assist, and SSH through Visual Studio Code, followed by new local and domain admin account creation.
- A second, unidentified threat actor operated concurrently in the same environment using DLL sideloading into legitimate Windows processes and custom backdoors, neither linked to Storm-2603. The layered activity from two actors obscured each other, complicating attribution and timeline reconstruction.
- The driver NSecKrnl.sys was loaded to tamper with memory and disable endpoint protections before subsequent activity, a classic BYOVD move that blind-spots EDR before the heavier tooling arrives.
- DART confirmed at least two victim organizations through lateral movement forensics, and any unpatched internet-facing SharePoint server remains exposed.

item.title: Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel
item.description:
Chaos ransomware's msaRAT routes all C2 traffic through Chrome DevTools Protocol and WebRTC, making the RAT process itself invisible to network monitors while burying attacker comms inside legitimate browser activity.
Key findings:
- Delivered via curl.exe over plain HTTP on port 443 (bypassing port-only firewall rules) as update_ms.msi to C:\programdata\, which drops lib.dll directly into memory via a custom MSI action. The RAT exports a single function, RUN, and impersonates a Windows update in installer metadata.
- msaRAT launches Chrome or Edge in headless mode via CreateProcessW, injects JavaScript through CDP Runtime.evaluate after bypassing CSP, and signals the C2 through Cloudflare Workers endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers[.]dev. Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio[.]com) relays all subsequent WebRTC DataChannel traffic, intentionally omitting ICE candidates so no P2P path forms and the attacker's real IP never appears in traffic.
- All network activity from the RAT process is limited to 127.0.0[.]1. External comms appear as browser-originated WebRTC, double-encrypted with ChaCha-Poly1305 over DTLS. The C2 IP 172.86.126[.]18 appears only in the initial MSI download.
- Hunt for headless browser processes (HeadlessChrome User-Agent) making WebRTC connections, MSI files writing DLLs to ProgramData, and curl.exe dropping installers. ClamAV sig Win.Downloader.ChaosRaas-10060321-0 and Snort rules SID 66839-66841 (v2), 301587 (v3) cover this.

item.title: wp2shell hits WordPress: detecting pre-auth RCE from plugin drop to command execution
item.description:
CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137 chain into pre-auth RCE on WordPress 6.9.0-6.9.4 and 7.0.0-7.0.1. Public PoCs hit GitHub within hours of July 17 disclosure; active scanning and exploitation confirmed in telemetry.
- wp2shell abuses route confusion in WordPress Core's REST batch endpoint (/wp-json/batch/v1 or /?rest_route=/batch/v1, no plugins required) to reach a pre-auth SQL injection primitive, then escalates via SQLi-to-administrator bridge and plugin upload, or direct INTO OUTFILE webshell drop. Both paths land attacker-controlled PHP on disk, then shell execution through the web stack. MITRE: T1190, T1505.003, T1059.
- The staging sequence leaves a durable file trail: apache2 writes temp-write-test-* probe files under wp-content/, a zip lands under wp-content/uploads/, PHP unpacks to wp-content/upgrade/wp2shell_<hex>/, then moves into wp-content/plugins/wp2shell_<hex>/. The PoC self-deletes the plugin post-execution, so a missing wp2shell_* folder does not clear the host if process alerts already fired.
- Elastic's lab run produced 12 alerts across four rules: PHP File Creation in WordPress Plugin Directory (earliest signal, catches the drop), Payload Execution by Web Server (fires and kills dash when apache2 spawns it), and Suspicious/Unusual Command Execution via Web Server (SIEM depth on id, whoami, hostname, SUID enumeration). The hex suffix in plugin names is fragile; the apache2-to-dash parent-child relationship is not.

item.title: Rondo Meets Geoserver, (Wed, Jul 22nd)
item.description:
CVE-2024-36401 still being actively scanned in the wild: the Rondo botnet is hitting GeoServer installs via OGC filter RCE, dropping a shell script through a multi-stage wget/curl chain.
Key findings:
- CVE-2024-36401 is an XPath expression injection in GeoServer's OGC filter evaluation, allowing unauthenticated RCE via a crafted GetPropertyValue WFS request. The payload calls java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime() directly in the valueReference parameter, no auth required.
- The attack chain: URL-encoded exec() call in the WFS request, base64-encoded second stage decoded and piped to sh, fetching rondo.zyt[.]sh from 45.153.34[.]153 via wget, busybox wget, or curl as fallbacks.
- The C2 at 45.153.34[.]153 now returns a taunting HTML comment ("You won't find it here"), suggesting the payload was removed or the bot was evicted, but persistent implants may remain.
- GeoServer is common in government, utilities, and research environments running geospatial infrastructure, making exposed instances high-value targets for botnet recruitment.
Hunt your web logs for GetPropertyValue requests containing exec( or base64 strings in the valueReference parameter. Check for outbound connections to 45.153.34[.]153 and unexpected sh or bash processes spawned from the GeoServer JVM. Patch to GeoServer 2.23.6 / 2.24.4 or later if not already done.

item.title: Opening the Black Box: Agentless Threat Detection for Virtual Appliances
item.description:
FortiGate devices are a prime attacker target: internet-facing, highly privileged, and invisible to traditional EDR. Wiz outlines agentless detection playbooks covering the full post-exploitation chain.
Key findings:
- 51.9% of cloud environments run at least one virtual appliance; 12% run FortiGate specifically. The 2026 FortiBleed campaign compromised credentials for roughly 75,000 devices across 194 countries. Salt Typhoon exploited CVE-2023-48788; UNC3886 used CVE-2022-41328 to deploy the CASTLETAP backdoor via FortiManager script abuse, then pivoted to VMware ESXi. A zero-day, CVE-2026-24858, was exploited to authenticate via SSO, create super_admin accounts, and delete logs.
- Post-compromise persistence follows a fast pattern: attackers authenticate via FortiCloud SSO using disposable addresses (support@openmail[.]pro, cloud-noc@mail[.]io), create a local admin (ssl-admin, backupadmin, helpdesk) with super_admin profile, MFA disabled, and trusthost=0.0.0.0/0, then immediately run "show full-configuration" to extract reversible-encrypted credentials, all within 10 minutes.
- Key log IDs to ingest: 32001/32002/32003 (auth), 44547 (object config, covers account creation, NAT/VIP, cert changes), 44548 (CLI commands executed), 32095 (config download via GUI), 32052 (FortiManager script push). For lateral movement, hunt subtype=local traffic logs for ICMP (proto=1) or unexpected outbound connections originating from the firewall itself.

item.title: Intercepting Android WebView traffic under new certificate validity requirement by Chromium
item.description:
Burp Suite's 1-year proxy cert now fails Android WebView interception silently. Chromium's cert validity enforcement (CERT_VALIDITY_TOO_LONG, net_error -213) breaks TLS interception without any app-side pinning in place.
Key findings:
- Chromium in Android WebView enforces max cert lifetimes per CA/B Forum Baseline Requirements. Certs issued on or after March 15, 2026 must be 200 days or fewer. Burp generates a 365-day cert (notAfter one year out), which now hard-fails with SSL error code 1, net_error -213 in logcat. mitmproxy generates shorter-lived certs and intercepts cleanly.
- The check lives in CertVerifyProc::HasTooLongValidity inside libwebviewchromium.so. It applies to any leaf cert marked as issued by a known root, meaning your Burp CA cert alone does not exempt the generated leaf from the validity window check.
- Three workarounds, easiest first: (1) uninstall WebView updates via adb shell dumpsys webviewupdate to revert to version 113; (2) chain mitmproxy on port 9090 as upstream proxy to Burp on port 8080 using --mode upstream with --ssl-insecure; (3) Frida-hook both cert_verify_proc at offset 0x3e015f8 and CachingCertVerifier::Verify at 0x3e00068 in libwebviewchromium.so after disabling multiprocess via adb shell cmd webviewupdate disable-multiprocess.
Before your next Android WebView assessment, confirm your proxy cert lifetime with openssl x509 -noout -dates.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2079945484970442916

item.title: Dolphin X Stealer Targets 300+ Apps and Profiles Users with AI
item.description:

On a developer machine, .env files and SSH directories often hold over-scoped, long-lived credentials reaching cloud consoles, build pipelines, and production environments.

This means the vendor touches every binary before delivery, enabling a tiered mutation engine that rewrites control flow, shuffles import tables, and rewrites PE timestamps, directly targeting hash-based blocklists and brittle YARA rules.
- The AI Profiler scores each infected host on app usage, browsing activity, and installed software, returning a ranked daily summary so operators can triage thousands of machines and focus on the highest-value targets first.
Detection should focus on behavior, not file hashes: explorer.exe running under a non-default desktop is a strong HVNC indicator regardless of packing. Keep long-lived credentials off disk and out of project directories.

item.title: Azure VM Command Execution using Third-Party Extensions – Chef
item.description:
Attackers with a single Azure RBAC permission can deploy a rogue Chef extension to any VM and execute arbitrary code as root, stealing Managed Identity tokens while blending into legitimate admin activity.
Key findings:
- The only permission needed is Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write, held by Owner, Contributor, Log Analytics Contributor, Virtual Machine Contributor, and several lesser-known roles including Defender for Servers and Desktop Virtualization Contributor. On engagements, Domain Controllers frequently run as Azure VMs, making any principal with this permission effectively a Domain Admin.
- Attack chain: stand up chef-zero (no auth, no input validation) on a public IP, craft a malicious cookbook that curls the IMDS endpoint at 169.254.169.254 to steal the Managed Identity OAuth token and exfiltrates it OOB, then deploy ChefClient or LinuxChefClient extension via az vm extension set pointing bootstrap_options.chef_server_url at the rogue server.
- Host artifacts to hunt: on Linux, check /var/lib/waagent/Chef.Bootstrap.WindowsAzure.LinuxChefClient-[version]/config/0.settings for a suspicious chef_server_url and /var/log/azure/Chef.Bootstrap.WindowsAzure.LinuxChefClient/chef-client.log for executed commands. On Windows, C:\chef\0.settings and C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\Plugins\Chef.Bootstrap.WindowsAzure.ChefClient\[version]\chef-client.log hold the same evidence.

item.title: Detecting Emails Sent Using Unexpected Languages (+KQL Query)
item.description:
A KQL hunting query flags emails where the detected language mismatches the sender IP's expected country language, surfacing a low-signal indicator useful for layered phishing and BEC investigations.
Key details:
- The query uses Microsoft Sentinel's EmailEvents table, resolving SenderIPv4/IPv6 with geo_info_from_ip_address(), then comparing the detected EmailLanguage (first two characters, lowercased) against a country-to-language mapping loaded via externaldata() from a GitHub-hosted CSV, keeping maintenance outside the query itself.
- Country-language mappings are stored in a semicolon-delimited CSV, split into an array at runtime. Emails where the detected language is absent from that array and not flagged as unknown ("un"/"xx") become hunting candidates, scoped to low-volume senders (EmailCount < 10) to reduce noise.
- Tuning is built in: exclude high-FP countries, allowlist trusted sender domains, and adjust volume thresholds. The author explicitly cautions this is not a standalone phishing detector, its value comes when stacked with signals like newly registered domains, SPF/DKIM failures, or unusual sender behavior.
- The artifact cluster to chase: SenderIP, Country, DetectedLanguage, SenderDomains, ThreatTypes, and Subject lines, all surfaced per sender in the output summarize.
Takeaway: Pull the KQL from the report and run it against EmailEvents in Sentinel.

The "exploitarium" GitHub archive has grown to 35 project folders and 204 tracked files of uncoordinated PoC releases, with CVE-2026-55200 in libssh2 as its most critical output: a pre-auth heap out-of-bounds write reachable before credentials are checked.
- CVE-2026-55200 targets libssh2 through 1.11.1. An insufficient upper-bound check on packet_length in ssh2_transport_read() causes integer wrap, producing an undersized heap buffer. It is pre-authentication, no credentials or session state required. libssh2 is a transitive dependency of curl, Git, and PHP builds, so exposure reaches CI/CD pipelines and container images far beyond teams who knowingly ship it. Fix is upstream commit 97acf3d. Run SCA across build artifacts and vendored deps now.
- The archive is larger and more active than reported. Most coverage cited roughly 130 files; the current count is 204 across 35 folders as of this assessment, with additions landing at 2-3 folders per week through at least July 4, including PostgreSQL, Redis, Nextcloud, and Discourse findings.
- The methodology is not purely automated. 19 folders cover native memory-safety bugs (C/C++, kernel/driver), consistent with fuzzing. 13 folders target web-app and authentication logic: API key scoping, CSRF-driven privilege escalation, federated-share tokens, cache-key collisions. That split signals human-directed targeting alongside fuzzing.
- The archive has evolved into a multi-contributor pipeline.
